html:
A form of popular Japanese theatre with song, dance and drama, begun in Kyoto around 1603 by a woman performer named Izumo no Okuni. It became the great stage art of the townspeople of Tokugawa Japan.

Okuni and her troupe danced on the dry bed of the Kamo River, in bold, fashionable costume. Their shows were a hit, and other troupes, often linked to prostitution, copied them. The shogunate banned women from the stage in 1629, then young men, so adult men took all the roles. The actors who play women, the onnagata, became a highlight of the art.

Kabuki grew in Edo, Osaka and Kyoto in the late 1600s. It has bright costumes and makeup, a revolving stage, and a walkway through the audience. Plays told of historical feuds, samurai loyalty and the love affairs of merchants, some written by Chikamatsu Monzaemon. Actor families such as the Ichikawa passed down styles and names. Woodblock prints of star actors sold widely. Unlike the older and more austere Noh theatre, it was made for crowds, and it is still performed today.
sum: A form of popular Japanese theatre with song, dance and drama, begun in Kyoto around 1603 by a woman performer named Izumo no Okuni. It became the great stage art of the townspeople of Tokugawa Japan.
